options: null SIGTERM
0 null

questions.q: A customer's name is used to run an invoice program. Which call is safe?
questions.explain: execFile passes each argument straight to the program; no shell reads it, so characters like ; or $( ) mean nothing. Every other option hands the text to a shell, and removing one kind of quote does not stop the others.
options: execFile("render-invoice", ["--name", customer.name])
exec(`render-invoice --name "${customer.name}"`)
exec(`render-invoice --name '${customer.name.replaceAll('"', "")}'`)
spawn(`render-invoice --name ${customer.name}`, { shell: true })

questions.q: A child program produces a 300 MB CSV export on stdout. Which function should start it?
questions.explain: execFile and exec collect all output in memory before handing it over. For big output, spawn lets you process it piece by piece, for example piping it into a file, with constant memory.
options: spawn, reading child.stdout as a stream
execFile with maxBuffer: 400 * 1024 * 1024
exec, because it uses a shell
fork, because the output is big

questions.q: Your server has a SIGTERM handler that takes 45 seconds to finish. Kubernetes uses its default 30-second grace period. What happens?
questions.explain: SIGKILL cannot be caught or delayed. The grace period is a hard limit, so a shutdown must finish well within it, which is why the lesson's shutdown has its own shorter deadline.
options: After 30 seconds Kubernetes sends SIGKILL and the process dies mid-shutdown
Kubernetes waits until the handler finishes
The handler also receives SIGKILL and can finish
Node.js ignores the SIGTERM because a handler is running

questions.q: A container stops and Docker reports exit code 137. What does that tell you?
questions.explain: Shells and Docker report a death by signal as 128 + the signal number. 137 = 128 + 9, SIGKILL. The out-of-memory killer and an expired grace period both send SIGKILL.
options: The process was killed by signal 9 (SIGKILL), for example for using too much memory
The program called process.exit(137) after an error
The program crashed with an uncaught exception
The program handled SIGTERM and exited normally

questions.q: A report loops over 10 million orders and takes 2 seconds of pure calculation. A developer makes the function async. What changes?
questions.explain: async only lets a function pause while it waits for something with await. A loop that only calculates never pauses. Moving it to a worker thread is what frees the event loop.
options: Nothing useful: the loop still blocks the event loop for 2 seconds
The loop now runs in the background on another core
The loop is split into small pieces automatically
Other requests are now answered between iterations
It runs twice as fast

questions.q: Which job is the best fit for a worker thread?
questions.explain: Workers are for heavy JavaScript calculation. Waiting for databases and files is already handled by the event loop, and git is another program, which needs a child process.
options: Resizing thousands of images with a pure JavaScript image library
Waiting for 50 database queries at the same time
Running the git command
Reading a large file line by line

questions.q: What is the right thing to do in a process.on("uncaughtException") handler of a server?
questions.explain: The error stopped some code halfway, so the program's state may be broken: half-finished transfers, locks never released. A fresh process is the only state you can trust.
options: Log the error, stop taking new work and exit with a non-zero code so a supervisor restarts the server
Log the error and carry on as if nothing happened
Do nothing, so the server never crashes
Retry the function that threw

questions.q: You read a child's stdout line by line. Which event tells you that you have received every line?
questions.explain: "exit" fires when the process ends, but its output streams may still hold data. "close" fires after the process has ended and its streams are closed.
options: "close"
"exit"
"spawn"
"disconnect"

questions.q: execFile rejects with ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER. What happened?
questions.explain: The buffered functions keep all output in memory, up to maxBuffer (1 MiB by default). Past that limit the child is killed. Use spawn for large output.
options: The child printed more than maxBuffer bytes, so Node.js killed it
The child ran out of memory
The child's exit code was too large
The child tried to read from stdin

questions.q: Which order is right for a graceful shutdown of a payment server?
questions.explain: First stop new work, so the amount of work can only shrink. Then finish what was started, which may still need the database, and only then close the connections.
options: Stop accepting new requests, finish the requests in progress, close database connections, exit
Close database connections, finish the requests in progress, stop accepting new requests, exit
Exit at once, the platform will retry the requests
Finish the requests in progress, then keep accepting new ones until none arrive

questions.q: Why is the shutdown deadline timer unref()ed?
questions.explain: An active timer keeps a Node.js process running. unref() tells Node.js not to count it, so the timer only matters when other work is still holding the process open.
options: So that it does not keep the process alive: a quick shutdown exits at once instead of waiting for the timer
So that it fires earlier
So that it cannot be cleared
So that it survives SIGKILL
So that it runs in a worker thread

questions.q: Your logs show MaxListenersExceededWarning: ... 11 reloaded listeners added to [PriceList]. What should you do first?
questions.explain: The warning is a leak detector. The eleventh listener was added. Raising the limit only hides the leak until memory runs out.
options: Find the code that adds a listener repeatedly (for example once per request) and make it add once or remove it
Call setMaxListeners(1000) to silence it
Nothing: the eleventh listener was not added
Restart the server every hour

questions.q: In the supervisor you built, why does a job that crashed the worker twice go to the dead letters instead of being retried forever?
questions.explain: A job that crashes the worker every time is a poison job. Retrying it forever turns one bad invoice into a total outage. One retry covers a fluke; after that, set it aside for a person to look at.
options: Otherwise one bad job would crash every new worker and block all the jobs behind it
Because a worker can only be restarted twice in Node.js
Because dead-letter jobs run faster
Because crashed jobs are always caused by the network

questions.q: A child prints ready and then registers process.on("SIGTERM", …). The parent sends SIGTERM as soon as it reads ready. What can happen?
questions.explain: This is a race: whether the handler exists depends on which process happens to be faster. Announce readiness only after everything, handlers included, is set up.
options: Sometimes the signal arrives before the handler exists, and the child is killed instead of shutting down gracefully
Nothing, because Node.js queues signals until a handler exists
The parent receives the SIGTERM instead
The child always ignores the signal

questions.q: You await once(worker, "exit"), and the worker throws an error before it exits. What happens at the await?
questions.explain: events.once treats "error" specially and rejects with it. If a failure is expected, listen for "error" yourself and wait for "exit" with a plain promise, as the lesson's worker example does.
options: It throws the worker's error, because once rejects when "error" is emitted while it waits
It resolves with exit code 1 and ignores the error
It waits forever
It resolves with the error object

questions.q: execFile("invoice-pdf-renderer", []) rejects with error.code === "ENOENT". What does that mean?
questions.explain: ENOENT means "no such file". The program is not installed or not on the PATH. There is no exit code, because no process ever started. Checking required programs at startup turns this into a clear message.
options: The program could not be found, so it never ran
The program ran and exited with an error
The program's output file is missing
The program took too long

questions.q: What happens when you postMessage({ total() {} }) to a worker?
questions.explain: Structured cloning copies data, not code. Send plain data and let the worker's own code act on it.
options: It throws a DataCloneError: functions cannot be copied between threads
The function is sent and runs in the worker
The function is silently dropped and {} arrives
The worker receives the function's source code as a string

questions.q: Why start a Node.js server in Docker with CMD ["node", "server.js"] rather than through a shell script?
questions.explain: With a wrapper shell, the shell receives the signal and may not pass it on. Node.js then never hears SIGTERM, and Docker kills it with SIGKILL after the grace period.
options: So that SIGTERM from Docker reaches the Node.js process and its shutdown handler runs
So that Node.js starts faster
Because shell scripts cannot start Node.js
So that the server can use more memory

questions.q: A parent process is killed with SIGKILL while two child processes run. What happens to the children?
questions.explain: Killing a parent does not kill its children. A graceful shutdown should stop its children itself, and a SIGKILL gives it no chance to, which is another reason to keep shutdowns short.
options: They keep running as orphans unless something else stops them
They are killed automatically with SIGKILL too
They receive SIGTERM and shut down gracefully
They pause until the parent is restarted

questions.q: A server starts a new worker thread for every incoming report request. What is the main risk?
questions.explain: Each worker is a whole JavaScript engine. A fixed-size pool, usually about one worker per core, queues extra work instead of multiplying the cost.
options: A burst of requests starts hundreds of workers, each with its own memory, and the server runs out of memory or thrashes
Workers cannot be started more than once
Reports come back in the wrong order
The main thread gets blocked by the workers

questions.q: You spawn a program that does not exist and only listen for "close". What goes wrong?
questions.explain: A child that fails to start emits "error". Like on any emitter, an "error" event with no listener throws. Always listen for "error" on child processes.
options: The child emits "error" with nobody listening, which throws and crashes your program
Nothing, "close" fires with code 127
The spawn call returns null
Node.js installs the program

questions.q: What should you know about signals on Windows?
questions.explain: Windows has no real POSIX signals. Write your shutdown for SIGTERM and SIGINT, and test it on Linux, where servers usually run.
options: They are emulated: Ctrl + C gives SIGINT in a console, and child.kill() always ends the child forcefully
They work exactly as on Linux
Node.js cannot start child processes on Windows
Windows sends SIGTERM when you close a window

questions.q: Write a tiny Emitter class with on(name, fn), off(name, fn) and emit(name, ...args). emit calls the listeners in order and returns true if there was at least one, like Node.js.
questions.explain: A map from event name to an array of functions is the whole idea. emit copies the array before looping, so a listener that removes itself during emit does not make the loop skip the next one; Node.js does the same.
questions.expected:
false
paid ORD-2
receipt ORD-2
true
receipt ORD-3

questions.q: Add a once(name, fn) method to this emitter: the listener runs on the first event only and then removes itself.
questions.explain: Register a wrapper function that first removes itself (the wrapper, not fn, since the wrapper is what was registered) and then calls the real listener.

questions.q: Write describeExit(code, signal) for a supervisor's log. A normal exit gives exited with code N. A signal gives killed by NAME (shell reports M), where M is 128 plus the signal's number. Use the numbers in SIGNALS.
questions.explain: Node.js gives you either an exit code or a signal name, never both. Shells and Docker combine them into one number, 128 + signal, which is why 143 and 137 are worth recognising.
questions.expected:
exited with code 0
exited with code 1
killed by SIGTERM (shell reports 143)
killed by SIGKILL (shell reports 137)

questions.q: Write splitRanges(total, parts) that splits the numbers 0 … total - 1 into parts ranges [start, end) for workers. The last range may be shorter; no range may go past total.
questions.explain: Rounding the size up with Math.ceil guarantees every number is covered; Math.min stops the last range at total. Each range can then go to its own worker, as in the lesson's report pool.

questions.q: Write createShutdown(). It returns a function onSignal(name): the first call returns graceful: NAME, every later call returns force: NAME (the impatient second Ctrl + C).
questions.explain: A closure keeps the shuttingDown flag private to each shutdown controller. In a real program the graceful branch would stop new work and start the deadline timer, and the force branch would call process.exit(1).
questions.expected:
graceful: SIGTERM
force: SIGINT
force: SIGINT
graceful: SIGINT

questions.q: Write decide(failures, jobId, maxCrashes) for the supervisor. It records one more crash for the job in the failures map and returns "retry", or "dead-letter" once the job has crashed maxCrashes times.
questions.explain: Counting per job, not in total, matters: one poison job should not use up the retries of healthy jobs. ?? 0 starts a job with no record at zero.

questions.q: Write withTimeout(promise, ms, message): it resolves like promise, or rejects with new Error(message) if ms milliseconds pass first. Clear the timer either way.
questions.explain: Promise.race settles with whichever promise settles first. Clearing the timer in finally matters in Node.js: a forgotten timer keeps the process alive, and a thousand forgotten timers keep a thousand closures in memory.
questions.expected:
invoice rendered
error: renderer timed out

questions.q: Write invoiceArgs(invoice) that returns the argument array for execFile("render-invoice", args): ["--id", id, "--amount", amount-as-text]. Throw Error("bad amount") unless the amount is a positive integer (kobo). The name is passed as it is: no quoting needed, since no shell reads it.
questions.explain: Each value is its own array element, so the dangerous-looking name is just text for the program. Validating the amount is still your job: execFile prevents injection, not bad data.
